title: Branch, switch, and the two kinds of merge
summary: A branch is a 17-byte file containing a commit id. Create one, commit on it, and watch the difference between a fast-forward merge and a real merge commit.
mental_model: A branch is not a copy of your code. It is a sticky note with a commit id written on it. `switch` moves HEAD to a different sticky note and rewrites your working tree to match. That is the entire feature.

write.content:
def run_pump(seconds):
    print('pump on for', seconds)

steps.title: Prove a branch is just a file
steps.why: Before any theory, look at the thing itself. `refs/heads/main` is a file whose entire content is one commit id. Everything you will ever hear about branching is built on that.

steps.title: Create a branch and move onto it
steps.why: `switch -c` creates the sticky note and points HEAD at it. No files change, no commits are made — both branches name the same commit right now.

steps.title: Commit on the branch
steps.why: Now the two sticky notes diverge: feature/lighting advances, main stays put. Only the branch you have checked out moves when you commit.

steps.title: Look at the divergence
steps.why: `main..feature/lighting` means "commits reachable from the second, not the first". This two-dot range syntax shows up everywhere — in log, diff, and code review tooling.

steps.title: Fast-forward merge
steps.why: main has not moved since the branch point, so git does not need to create a merge commit — it just slides the main pointer forward. History stays a straight line. This is why some teams love fast-forward and others ban it: it erases the fact a branch existed.

verify.label: main now contains the lighting commit

steps.title: Now force a real merge commit
steps.why: `--no-ff` tells git to make a merge commit even when it could fast-forward. The merge commit has two parents, which is what makes the branch visible in history forever.

verify.label: HEAD is a merge commit (two parents)
verify.hint: use git merge --no-ff so git cannot slide the pointer

steps.title: Clean up the merged branches
steps.why: `branch -d` refuses to delete a branch that is not merged — a safety net worth trusting. `-D` overrides it, and is how people lose work.

verify.label: the last merge was a real merge commit, not a fast-forward
the merged lighting branch was deleted

pitfalls: `git switch` with uncommitted changes carries them along — that surprises people who expect isolation. Commit or stash first.
`git branch feature` creates the branch but does NOT move to it. `git switch -c feature` does both.
Deleting a branch never deletes commits. They stay reachable through the reflog for weeks.
